1b.html:
Sol-gel steps (slides 42-44): solution \rightarrow sol \rightarrow gel \rightarrow dried gel \rightarrow ceramic.

  1. Sol formation: a metal alkoxide \mathrm{M(OR)_x} dissolved in its alcohol.
  2. Hydrolysis with added water (acid or base catalyst):
\mathrm{M(OR)_x} + x\,\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{M(OH)_x} + x\,\mathrm{ROH}
  1. Condensation to metal-oxygen-metal bonds:
\mathrm{M{-}OH} + \mathrm{HO{-}M} \rightarrow \mathrm{M{-}O{-}M} + \mathrm{H_2O}, \qquad \mathrm{M{-}OR} + \mathrm{HO{-}M} \rightarrow \mathrm{M{-}O{-}M} + \mathrm{ROH}
  1. Gelation: the network spans the liquid (particulate or polymeric gel, slide 44).
  2. Ageing and drying: the network stiffens; the liquid is removed slowly, since capillary stress causes large shrinkage and cracks.
  3. Calcination or firing: organics burn out and the amorphous gel crystallises and densifies.

Water content, pH, temperature and catalyst set the rates and the gel structure.

2a.html:
Take the Schottky defect in an MO oxide such as MgO; the same four steps (reaction, equilibrium constant, electroneutrality, solve) work for any defect.

Step 1, defect reaction.

\mathrm{null} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{V_{Mg}^{\prime\prime}} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}

One cation and one anion site are vacated (site ratio 1:1 kept), charge (-2) + (+2) = 0.

Step 2, free energy. Forming n pairs on N sites of each sublattice costs n\Delta H and gains vibrational entropy n\Delta S and configurational entropy k\ln W, with W = [N!/n!(N-n)!]^2:

\Delta G = n\Delta H - nT\Delta S - 2kT\ln\frac{N!}{n!\,(N-n)!}

Using Stirling's approximation and setting \partial\Delta G/\partial n = 0:

\Delta H - T\Delta S = 2kT\ln\frac{N-n}{n} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{n}{N} \approx \exp\left(\frac{\Delta S}{2k}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H}{2kT}\right) \quad (n \ll N)

Step 3, equilibrium constant. The same result is the mass-action law for Step 1, with brackets as site fractions and the perfect crystal (null) at unit activity:

K_S = [\mathrm{V_{Mg}^{\prime\prime}}][\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] = \exp\left(-\frac{\Delta G}{kT}\right) = \exp\left(\frac{\Delta S}{k}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H}{kT}\right)

Step 4, electroneutrality: 2[\mathrm{V_{Mg}^{\prime\prime}}] = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}].

Step 5, solve.

\boxed{[\mathrm{V_{Mg}^{\prime\prime}}] = [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] = K_S^{1/2} = \exp\left(\frac{\Delta S}{2k}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H}{2kT}\right)}

Multiply by the sites per unit volume to get defects per \mathrm{cm^3}. A Frenkel pair gives the same form with \Delta H_F; a reaction that makes \nu defects gives [\,] \propto K^{1/\nu} (for \mathrm{M_2O_3} Schottky, [\mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime\prime}}] = 0.78\,K_S^{1/5}).

Influence of temperature

  1. \ln[\mathrm{V}] = \Delta S/2k - (\Delta H/2k)(1/T): a straight Arrhenius line of slope -\Delta H/2k, so the concentration rises exponentially with T. For MgO (\Delta H = 7.5\ \mathrm{eV}) [\mathrm{V}] = 1.4\times10^{-15} at 1273 K (7.6\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}), twelve times more 100 K higher; NaCl (2.3 eV) goes from 4.8\times10^{-20} at 300 K to 3.6\times10^{-7} at 900 K.
  2. These are equilibrium defects: present at any T > 0, they cannot be annealed out, and quenching freezes the high-temperature value.
  3. With an aliovalent impurity (\mathrm{CdCl_2} in NaCl), [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = [\mathrm{Cd_{Na}^{\bullet}}] + [\mathrm{V_{Cl}^{\bullet}}]. At high T the intrinsic term dominates; at low T the dopant fixes [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}], independent of T (extrinsic), while [\mathrm{V_{Cl}^{\bullet}}] = K_S/[\mathrm{Cd_{Na}^{\bullet}}] falls with slope -\Delta H/k.
  4. Hence diffusion has activation energy \Delta H_m + \Delta H/2 in the intrinsic range but only \Delta H_m in the extrinsic range.

Given: \mathrm{Fe_{1-y}O}, rock salt, a = 429\ \mathrm{pm} = 4.29\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}, \rho = 5.63\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}.

Assume: the oxygen sublattice is full (4 O per cubic cell, as in rock salt); the deficit is Fe vacancies, \mathrm{V_{Fe}^{\prime\prime}}, each compensated by two \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} (\mathrm{Fe_{Fe}^{\bullet}}), as slides 18-19 show. M_{\mathrm{Fe}} = 55.85, M_{\mathrm{O}} = 16.00\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}.

Find: (i) 1 - y; (ii) defects per \mathrm{cm^3}.

Solution

\begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{cell}} &= a^3 = (4.29\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm})^3 = 7.895\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3} \\ m_{\mathrm{cell}} &= \rho V_{\mathrm{cell}} = (5.63)(7.895\times10^{-23}) = 4.445\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{g} \\ m_{\mathrm{O}} &= \frac{4 \times 16.00}{6.022\times10^{23}} = 1.063\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{g} \\ n_{\mathrm{Fe}} &= \frac{(4.445 - 1.063)\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{g}}{55.85/6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{g}} = 3.647\ \text{Fe per cell} \\ 1 - y &= \frac{3.647}{4} = 0.912, \qquad y = 0.088 \end{aligned}

Defects: each cell has 4 - 3.647 = 0.353 vacant Fe sites, and electroneutrality 2[\mathrm{V_{Fe}^{\prime\prime}}] = [\mathrm{Fe_{Fe}^{\bullet}}] gives twice as many \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}:

\begin{aligned} n_{\mathrm{V}} &= \frac{0.353}{7.895\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}} = 4.47\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} \\ n_{\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}} &= 2n_{\mathrm{V}} = 8.9\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} \end{aligned}

Answer: (i) \mathrm{Fe_{0.912}O} (y = 0.088); (ii) 4.5\times10^{21} Fe vacancies per \mathrm{cm^3} (4.5\times10^{27}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}), with 8.9\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} per \mathrm{cm^3}, so about 19% of the Fe ions are \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}.

Rules: keep the host's site ratio, keep mass and keep zero net effective charge.

(i) Si into \mathrm{SiO_2}

Excess Si makes silicon-rich, oxygen-deficient \mathrm{SiO_{2-x}}. The Si atom takes a Si site; to keep the 1:2 ratio, two oxygen sites are created and left empty. Each \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} is +2, so four electrons are released:

\mathrm{Si(s)} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{SiO_2}\ } \mathrm{Si_{Si}^{\times}} + 2\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} + 4e^{\prime}

Mass: one Si each side. Sites: 1 Si to 2 O. Charge: 2(+2) + 4(-1) = 0. Mass action: K = [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}]^2 n^4/a_{\mathrm{Si}}, with n = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}].

Alternatives: Si as an interstitial, \mathrm{Si(s)} \to \mathrm{Si_i^{\bullet\bullet\bullet\bullet}} + 4e^{\prime}, or with the electrons kept on the vacancies, \mathrm{Si(s)} \to \mathrm{Si_{Si}^{\times}} + 2\mathrm{V_O^{\times}} (the neutral oxygen vacancy, a Si-Si bond in silica).

(ii) MgO into \mathrm{Al_2O_3}

\mathrm{Mg^{2+}} on an \mathrm{Al^{3+}} site is \mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}}. Two MgO bring two cations and two oxygens, but two Al sites need three O sites, so one O site stays vacant:

2\mathrm{MgO} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{Al_2O_3}\ } 2\mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}} + 2\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}

Mass: 2 Mg, 2 O. Sites: 2 Al to 3 O. Charge: 2(-1) + (+2) = 0; electroneutrality [\mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}}] = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}].

Alternative (interstitial compensation): 3\mathrm{MgO} \to 2\mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}} + \mathrm{Mg_i^{\bullet\bullet}} + 3\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}.

3b.html:
Why MgO insulates. Its band gap is about 7.8 eV and Mg has only one valence, so MgO cannot become non-stoichiometric. Intrinsic Schottky disorder costs \Delta H = 7.5\ \mathrm{eV} per pair, so even at 1000 °C [\mathrm{V_{Mg}^{\prime\prime}}] = \exp(-\Delta H/2kT) = 1.4\times10^{-15}: almost no mobile defects.

Effective way: aliovalent (extrinsic) doping. A higher-valence cation such as \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} or \mathrm{Al^{3+}} on a Mg site is compensated by Mg vacancies:

\mathrm{TiO_2} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{MgO}\ } \mathrm{Ti_{Mg}^{\bullet\bullet}} + \mathrm{V_{Mg}^{\prime\prime}} + 2\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}, \qquad [\mathrm{V_{Mg}^{\prime\prime}}] = [\mathrm{Ti_{Mg}^{\bullet\bullet}}]
\mathrm{Al_2O_3} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{MgO}\ } 2\mathrm{Al_{Mg}^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{V_{Mg}^{\prime\prime}} + 3\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}, \qquad [\mathrm{V_{Mg}^{\prime\prime}}] = \tfrac12[\mathrm{Al_{Mg}^{\bullet}}]

The vacancy content is now set by the dopant, not by \exp(-\Delta H/2kT). Since D_{\mathrm{Mg}} = D_0[\mathrm{V_{Mg}^{\prime\prime}}]\exp(-\Delta H_m/kT), 10% Ti gives 1.2\times10^{-12} against 1.7\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}} for pure MgO at 1000 °C. By Nernst-Einstein, \sigma_{\mathrm{ion}} = N(2e)^2D_{\mathrm{Mg}}/kT, so the \mathrm{Mg^{2+}} conductivity rises by about 10^{14}, and its activation energy falls from 5.75 eV to \Delta H_m = 2\ \mathrm{eV}.

Electronic alternative. Acceptor doping with \mathrm{Li_2O} under oxidising conditions makes holes, \mathrm{Li_2O} + \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2} \to 2\mathrm{Li_{Mg}^{\prime}} + 2\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + 2h^{\bullet}, giving p-type conduction.
pts: Explains the insulation: wide gap, fixed \mathrm{Mg^{2+}} valence, intrinsic [\mathrm{V}] \approx 10^{-15} at 1000 °C (\Delta H = 7.5\ \mathrm{eV})

Gives the electronic route: \mathrm{Li_2O} plus oxidation gives holes (\mathrm{Li_{Mg}^{\prime}} + h^{\bullet})

Given (Fig. for Q. 3(c)): tetragonal \mathrm{BaTiO_3}, a = 3.98 Å, c = 4.03 Å. Taking the corner \mathrm{Ba^{2+}} as fixed, \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} is displaced +6 pm along c, the \mathrm{O^{2-}} on the four side faces -6 pm, and the \mathrm{O^{2-}} on the top and bottom faces -9 pm. e = 1.602\times10^{-19} C.

Find: the maximum polarisation (dipole moment per \mathrm{cm^3}) and the charge stored per \mathrm{cm^2}.

Step 1, ions per cell. \mathrm{Ba^{2+}}: 8 \times \tfrac18 = 1; \mathrm{Ti^{4+}}: 1; top and bottom \mathrm{O^{2-}}: 2 \times \tfrac12 = 1; side \mathrm{O^{2-}}: 4 \times \tfrac12 = 2. Charge check: +2 + 4 - 2 - 4 = 0.

Step 2, dipole moments, \mu = q\delta. The anions move opposite to \mathrm{Ti^{4+}}, and (-2e)(-\delta) > 0, so every term adds in the +c direction (6\ \mathrm{pm} = 0.06\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}):

\begin{aligned} \mu_{\mathrm{Ti}} &= (4)(1.602\times10^{-19})(0.06\times10^{-8}) = 3.84\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{C\,cm} \\ \mu_{\mathrm{O,top}} &= (1)(2)(1.602\times10^{-19})(0.09\times10^{-8}) = 2.88\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{C\,cm} \\ \mu_{\mathrm{O,side}} &= (2)(2)(1.602\times10^{-19})(0.06\times10^{-8}) = 3.84\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{C\,cm} \\ \textstyle\sum\mu &= 1.06\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{C\,cm}\ \text{per cell} \end{aligned}

Step 3, polarisation. One dipole per cell, every cell aligned (a fully poled single domain):

\begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{cell}} &= a^2c = (3.98\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm})^2(4.03\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}) = 6.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3} \\ P &= \frac{\sum\mu}{V_{\mathrm{cell}}} = \frac{1.06\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{C\,cm}}{6.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}} = 1.66\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C\,cm\ per\ cm^3} \end{aligned}

That is 1.66\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C\,cm^{-2}} = 0.166\ \mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}.

Step 4, charge per unit area. Polarisation equals the bound surface charge density on the faces normal to c, \sigma = P (class note p 2). Electrodes on a poled crystal therefore hold

\frac{Q}{A} = P = 1.66\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C\,cm^{-2}} = \frac{1.66\times10^{-5}}{1.602\times10^{-19}} = 1.03\times10^{14}\ \text{electrons per cm}^2

Answer: maximum polarisation P \approx 1.66\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C\,cm} per \mathrm{cm^3} (0.166\ \mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}); charge stored \approx 1.66\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C} per \mathrm{cm^2}, about 10^{14} electronic charges.

• Use the tetragonal cell, a^2c, not a^3 or c^3; the cell is 4.03 Å along the polar axis.

4a.html:
The dielectric constant collects the contributions of four polarisation mechanisms, \varepsilon_r = 1 + \chi_e + \chi_i + \chi_d + \chi_s. Frequency and temperature change \varepsilon_r by switching these contributions on or off, or by changing their size.

Effect of frequency. Charges need time to follow the field, and heavier units over longer distances need more. As frequency rises, \varepsilon_r' therefore falls in steps:

  • space charge (interfacial) is lost above about 10^{2} to 10^{3} Hz;
  • dipolar (orientation) relaxes at about 10^{7} to 10^{9} Hz;
  • ionic is lost at its infrared resonance, about 10^{13} Hz;
  • electronic is lost at its ultraviolet resonance, about 10^{15} Hz.

At optical frequencies \varepsilon_r = n^2, and the loss \varepsilon'' peaks at every step.

Effect of temperature.

  • Electronic and ionic terms are nearly constant; only thermal expansion changes them a little.
  • The dipolar term falls with T, \alpha_d = \mu^2/3kT, because thermal agitation randomises the dipoles. In solids the dipoles may be frozen until a melting or order-disorder change frees them.
  • The space-charge term grows with T as ion mobility rises, so the low-frequency \varepsilon_r and loss climb.
  • In ferroelectrics \varepsilon_r peaks at the Curie point (\mathrm{BaTiO_3}, 120 °C, about 10^{4}) and falls above it as C/(T - T_0).
pts: States that \varepsilon_r sums the mechanism contributions and that each drops out above its own frequency, so \varepsilon_r' falls stepwise
Order and ranges: space charge about 10^{2} to 10^{3} Hz, dipolar about 10^{9} Hz, ionic about 10^{13} Hz, electronic about 10^{15} Hz; \varepsilon_r = n^2 at optical frequencies
Loss peaks at each step
Electronic and ionic contributions nearly independent of temperature
Dipolar contribution falls with temperature, \alpha_d = \mu^2/3kT
Space-charge contribution and loss rise with temperature

The materials. \mathrm{SiO_2} means crystalline \alpha-quartz: non-centrosymmetric, so piezoelectric, but non-polar, so not pyroelectric. The pyroelectric is taken as \mathrm{LiTaO_3} (slide 9); \mathrm{LaTiO_3} is centrosymmetric.

Piezoelectric quartz. Stress gives charge and a field gives strain, D = dT + \varepsilon E with d \approx 2.3\ \mathrm{pC\,N^{-1}}; quartz has low loss and a temperature-stable resonance.

  1. Crystal oscillators and filters. An AC voltage makes a thin plate vibrate and the vibration returns charge, so the circuit locks to the resonance, f = v/2t: the clock of watches, computers, phones and radios.
  2. Pressure and force sensors. A force gives a charge Q = dF; also accelerometers and microbalances.

Pyroelectric \mathrm{LiTaO_3}. Its spontaneous polarisation falls as it warms, so a temperature change drives a current, i = pA\,dT/dt, with p \approx 230\ \mu\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}.

  1. Infrared detectors: passive infrared intruder alarms, flame and fire detectors.
  2. Thermal imaging cameras and laser power meters.

5a.html:
Theory (Neel's collinear model). \mathrm{NiFe_2O_4} is inverse; \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} (3d^{10}, no moment) takes the A site and pushes \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} to B:

(\mathrm{Zn}_x\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x})_A[\mathrm{Ni}_{1-x}\mathrm{Fe}_{1+x}]_B\mathrm{O_4}

With A antiparallel to B, \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} 2\,\mu_B and \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} 5\,\mu_B:

n_B = M_B - M_A = \left[2(1-x) + 5(1+x)\right] - 5(1-x) = 2 + 8x

So the theory predicts 6\,\mu_B at x = 0.5, rising linearly to 10\,\mu_B for \mathrm{ZnFe_2O_4}.

Experiment. The measured moment follows this line only up to x \approx 0.4, peaks near x \approx 0.4 to 0.5, and then falls. \mathrm{ZnFe_2O_4} (x = 1) is not ferrimagnetic at all: it is antiferromagnetic below about 10 K and paramagnetic at room temperature. This is the anomaly.

Explanation.

  1. Assumption that fails. The Neel model needs the A-B exchange (A-O-B about 125^\circ, strong) to dominate the B-B exchange (90^\circ, weak), so that all B moments stay parallel. Both are antiferromagnetic.
  2. Dilution of A. Each B site has 6 nearest A sites. As Zn replaces A-site \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}, the number of magnetic A neighbours, and so the A-B molecular field on each B ion, falls roughly as (1-x), while the B-B field does not.
  3. Local frustration. Some B ions lose all their magnetic A neighbours (probability about x^6, already 0.26 at x = 0.8). Coupled only to other B ions, their moments turn antiparallel to the B majority.
  4. Yafet-Kittel canting. Collectively, the B sublattice splits into two halves, B_1 and B_2, canted by \pm\alpha_{YK} from the direction antiparallel to A (a triangular arrangement):
n_B = M_B\cos\alpha_{YK} - M_A

\alpha_{YK} grows with x and reaches 90^\circ at x = 1, when the B moments cancel and n_B \to 0.

  1. Lower Curie temperature. The weakened A-B exchange lowers T_C, so room-temperature moments fall even faster than the 0 K values.

Neutron diffraction on Zn-rich ferrites confirms the canted B moments. The anomaly is therefore the breakdown of the collinear two-sublattice model at high dilution.

Yafet-Kittel triangular arrangement: B_1, B_2 canted by \pm\alpha_{YK}, sketched
n_B = M_B\cos\alpha_{YK} - M_A, with \alpha_{YK} \to 90^\circ and n_B \to 0 as x \to 1
Curie temperature falls with Zn, lowering room-temperature values further
Concludes: the anomaly is the breakdown of the collinear model (supported by neutron diffraction)

5b.fix:
Slide 22 attributes the "magnetic locking" that keeps the train stable and centred to the Meissner effect. Complete flux expulsion only repels; it gives no restoring force sideways. Locking comes from flux pinning: in a type II superconductor between H_{c1} and H_{c2}, flux vortices are held by defects, so the superconductor resists any change of position relative to the magnet. In the coil-type train that slide 22 itself describes, neither effect acts: the centring comes from the cross-connected (null-flux) guideway coils.

Slide 13 gives "H_c \sim 1 tesla" for type I superconductors. Their critical fields are far lower: about 0.01 T for Al, 0.03 T for Sn, 0.04 T for Hg and 0.08 T for Pb, all below 0.1 T. Only type II materials reach several tesla (H_{c2} about 30 T for \mathrm{Nb_3Sn}).
5b.html:
Meissner effect. Below T_c (and below the critical field) a superconductor expels magnetic flux from its interior, whether the field was applied before or after cooling (slides 3, 5):

B = \mu_0(H + M) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad M = -H, \qquad \chi = -1

It is a perfect diamagnet. A normal conductor's eddy currents decay and the field soaks in; in a superconductor the screening currents never decay. They flow in a surface layer of thickness set by the London penetration depth,

\lambda_L = \sqrt{\frac{m}{\mu_0 n_s e^2}} \approx 50\ \text{nm for } n_s = 10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}},

and their field cancels the applied one inside, acting like a mirror-image magnet with like pole facing the real magnet.

Why this levitates. The field lines are squeezed between magnet and superconductor; the compressed field pushes on the surface with magnetic pressure

p = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}

For B = 0.5 T, p \approx 99.5 kPa, about 10 t per \mathrm{m^2}. The magnet rises until the repulsion equals its weight; the force falls with gap, so the height is self-adjusting.

Type I and type II (slide 13). Type I (Pb, Hg) expels flux fully up to H_c (below about 0.1 T) and then turns normal. Type II ceramics (YBCO, T_c = 92 K) expel flux fully up to H_{c1}; between H_{c1} and H_{c2} flux enters as vortices, which defects pin. Pinning locks the gap and stops sideways drift, so the levitation is stable and can carry heavy loads in strong fields.

Maglev train.

  • HTS maglev: YBCO blocks in liquid-nitrogen cryostats (77 K) under the car, over a permanent-magnet track: flux expulsion and pinning lift and centre the car with no power or control, even at rest.
  • Superconducting maglev (Japan): NbTi coils on the train carry persistent current (zero resistance, no power). Moving past normal-metal guideway coils, they induce currents whose opposing field lifts the train about 10 cm above about 150 km/h. Guideway coils with AC form a linear synchronous motor for propulsion and braking.
  • Benefits: no friction or wear, low noise and maintenance, speeds above 500 km/h (record 603 km/h), cheap liquid-nitrogen cooling for ceramics (slide 23).

Conclusion: the assertion holds for a superconductor levitating over magnets (Meissner expulsion plus pinning); in the coil-type train, zero resistance gives the strong magnets and electromagnetic induction does the lifting.

Type I against type II: H_c, H_{c1}, H_{c2}, mixed state
Flux pinning in type II ceramics gives stable locking
Maglev example: YBCO over a magnet track, or SC coils inducing guideway currents with a gap of about 10 cm
Propulsion and braking by a linear synchronous motor; benefits (no friction, over 500 km/h, liquid-nitrogen cooling)

6a.html:
A ceramic fails from its worst flaw, \sigma_f = K_{IC}/(Y\sqrt{\pi c}), and pores are the commonest processing flaw (slides 2-3).

1. Porosity. Strength falls much faster than density. On slide 3 (alumina) strength drops from about 220 MPa at 3% porosity to about 100 MPa at 18%, while density falls by only about 15%. Pores:

  • remove load-bearing cross-section;
  • concentrate stress and start cracks;
  • lower E and the fracture energy, so K_{IC} falls.

An empirical fit is

\sigma = \sigma_0\,e^{-nP}, \qquad n \approx 4 \text{ to } 7

(the slide's curve gives n \approx 5), so 10% porosity already costs 33 to 50% of the strength.

2. Pore shape. For an elliptical pore with semi-axis a across the stress and b along it (Inglis):

\sigma_{max} = \sigma\left(1 + \frac{2a}{b}\right)
  • A smooth, isolated spherical pore (final-stage sintering) is blunt, \sigma_{max} \approx 2\sigma: least harmful.
  • Flat pores lying across the stress, cusped pores at grain edges and triple junctions, and irregular interconnected (open) porosity have large a/b and act almost like cracks.
  • Pores elongated along the stress do little; large pores, clusters and surface pores are worst.

3. Pore-crack combination. A pore alone is blunt, but small cracks at its rim (machining damage, thermal-expansion mismatch, grain-boundary facets) sit in its raised stress. Pore and crack then act as one flaw of half-length about pore radius R plus crack length a:

\sigma_f \approx \frac{K_{IC}}{Y\sqrt{\pi(R + a)}}

With K_{IC} = 4\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}} and Y = 1, a 10\ \mu\mathrm{m} crack alone gives 714 MPa; on a 50\ \mu\mathrm{m} diameter pore (R + a = 35\ \mu\mathrm{m}) it gives 381 MPa, about half. A pore beside a large grain acts the same way (flaw about pore plus grain).

Conclusion: high strength needs a dense, fine-grained body with few small, rounded, isolated pores (hot pressing, HIP) and a good surface finish.
pts: Strength falls much faster than density with porosity, with the slide 3 example (alumina about 220 MPa to about 100 MPa near 18% porosity)
Reasons: less load-bearing area, stress concentration and crack initiation at pores, lower E and fracture energy
Empirical law \sigma = \sigma_0 e^{-nP} with n \approx 4 to 7
Inglis \sigma_{max} = \sigma(1 + 2a/b): the stress raised by a pore depends on its shape and orientation
Spherical isolated pores are blunt (about 2\sigma) and least harmful; flat, cusped or interconnected pores across the stress act like cracks; large, clustered or surface pores are worst
A pore with rim cracks acts as one flaw of size R + a, \sigma_f = K_{IC}/[Y\sqrt{\pi(R + a)}]
Shows the size of the effect (strength about halved in the example) or notes the pore plus large grain flaw
Conclusion: dense, fine-grained bodies with small, rounded, isolated pores (hot pressing, HIP) and good finishing

6a.watch:
• "Discuss" needs all three parts with a reason each, not only "porosity lowers strength".
  • Slide 3 values are read off the figure (about \pm 10 MPa); the exponent n depends on pore shape and stacking, which is why it varies from 4 to 7 or more.
  • A clean pore is not a crack: taking c = R for a pore with no rim cracks overestimates its damage. A spherical cavity raises the stress about 2 times, a cylindrical hole in a plate 3 times.
  • The pore-crack rule c_{eff} \approx R + a holds once a is comparable to R; for a very short rim crack the crack simply sees about 2\sigma to 3\sigma.

6b.fix: Slide 13 gives the monoclinic cell volume as about 139.3\ \text{\AA}^3, but its own lattice parameters give V = abc\sin\beta = 5.15 \times 5.21 \times 5.31 \times \sin 99.2^\circ = 140.6\ \text{\AA}^3. Against the tetragonal 134.2\ \text{\AA}^3 (the same four-formula cell), the t to m expansion is then about 4.8%, not 3.8%; the usual quoted value is 4 to 5% (Carter quotes about 3%). The tetragonal row also mixes cells: a = 3.60\ \text{\AA} is the two-formula primitive cell (67.1\ \text{\AA}^3), while 134.2\ \text{\AA}^3 belongs to the four-formula cell with a\sqrt{2} = 5.09\ \text{\AA}.
6b.html:
Basis. Zirconia is monoclinic (m) up to about 1170^\circ\mathrm{C}, tetragonal (t) up to about 2370^\circ\mathrm{C} and cubic (c) above. The t to m change is martensitic (diffusionless, athermal) with a volume increase of about 4 to 5% (from the slide 13 lattice parameters; see Correction) and a shear strain of about 0.16. \mathrm{Y_2O_3} lowers the transformation temperature because \mathrm{Y^{3+}} on \mathrm{Zr^{4+}} sites creates oxygen vacancies:

\mathrm{Y_2O_3} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{ZrO_2}\ } 2\mathrm{Y_{Zr}^{\prime}} + 3\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}

With about 3 to 8 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3} (slide 15), t is kept at room temperature as fine precipitates in a cubic matrix (PSZ) or as fine grains (TZP). It is metastable: held only by the elastic constraint of its surroundings and by a size below the critical size (a few tenths of a micrometre, larger at higher yttria content).

Mechanism (slide 14).

  1. The tensile stress field of a crack relieves the constraint and supplies the missing driving force, so t particles in a zone of half-width w around the tip transform to m.
  2. Their expansion is resisted by the untransformed material, so the zone and the crack wake are in compression. This closes the crack and lowers the stress intensity at the tip (shielding):
K_{tip} = K_{applied} - \Delta K_T, \qquad \Delta K_T = A\,V_t\,\varepsilon^T E\,w^{1/2}

with A \approx 1, V_t the fraction of transformable t, \varepsilon^T the transformation strain and E the modulus (Carter).

  1. The transformation absorbs energy; the wake grows as the crack advances (rising R-curve). K_{IC} rises from about 3\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}} (cubic) to 6 to 15\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}, and strength rises too.

Elevated temperature. The chemical driving force for t to m, \Delta G_{\mathrm{chem}} = G_m - G_t, shrinks as the temperature rises towards the t/m transformation temperature, so t becomes more stable. A higher crack-tip stress is needed, the zone w shrinks and \Delta K_T falls; by about 800 to 1000^\circ\mathrm{C} the toughening is largely lost and K_{IC} approaches the cubic value. Long holds also coarsen the t precipitates past the critical size (they turn m on cooling), and Y-TZP held at 150 to 300^\circ\mathrm{C} in moist air degrades by spontaneous surface t to m. PSZ is a room- and moderate-temperature material.

Full stabilisation with rare-earth oxides. With about 8 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3} or more (or other rare-earth oxides such as \mathrm{Yb_2O_3}, \mathrm{Gd_2O_3}, \mathrm{Sc_2O_3}), the cubic fluorite phase is stable down to room temperature (FSZ). No metastable t is left, nothing transforms at a crack tip, and K_{IC} stays about 2 to 3\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}: transformation toughening is lost. FSZ is used for its oxygen-ion conductivity (oxygen sensors, SOFC electrolytes), not for toughness.

7a.html:
Ceramics fail in tension from surface flaws, \sigma_f = K_{IC}/(Y\sqrt{\pi c}). Pre-stressing lowers the tension the flaws feel; crack deflection raises K_{IC}.

Pre-stressing. The surface is given a residual compressive stress \sigma_r, balanced by tension in the core. An applied tensile stress must first cancel it before surface flaws open:

\sigma_{f,\text{apparent}} \approx \sigma_f + \lvert\sigma_r\rvert
  • Thermal tempering of glass: heat above T_g, blast with cold air. The surface stiffens first; the hotter core contracts later and pulls the surface into compression.
  • Ion exchange: larger \mathrm{K^+} replaces \mathrm{Na^+} in the surface below T_g; the crowded layer is compressed (several hundred MPa).
  • Low-expansion glaze or surface layer: a glaze with smaller \alpha than the body is compressed on cooling (about 70 MPa, Carter).
  • Surface transformation: grinding TZP turns surface t to m, and the expansion compresses the surface.

If a crack penetrates the layer into the tensile core, the stored energy is released and tempered glass breaks into small dice.

Crack deflection (slide 12). Second-phase particles, platelets, whiskers, elongated grains (self-reinforced \mathrm{Si_3N_4}), weak interfaces or thermal-mismatch stress fields tilt and twist the crack out of the plane normal to the stress.

  • The tilted crack is loaded in mixed mode, so its opening-mode K_I is lower than the applied value: more load is needed.
  • The longer, tortuous path creates more fracture surface and absorbs more energy.
  • Rods and platelets deflect more than spheres.
pts: Pre-stressing puts the surface in residual compression that the applied tension must cancel first, \sigma_{f,\text{apparent}} \approx \sigma_f + \lvert\sigma_r\rvert
Thermal tempering: surface cools and stiffens first, the core contracts later, giving surface compression and core tension
A second method: ion exchange (\mathrm{K^+} for \mathrm{Na^+}), low-expansion glaze or surface t to m in TZP
Balancing core tension: a crack reaching the core releases the stored energy (dicing of tempered glass)
Crack deflection: particles, whiskers, elongated grains or weak interfaces tilt and twist the crack out of its plane
Tilted crack is in mixed mode, local K_I falls below the applied value
Longer path, more fracture surface and energy absorbed, so K_{IC} rises
Links both to strength: pre-stress raises the apparent strength at the same K_{IC}; deflection raises K_{IC}, so strength rises for the same flaw

• Stress profile: compression at both surfaces, tension in the core, and the reduced net tension at the loaded surface.
  • Crack path: tilted and twisted around particles or elongated grains, compared with the straight path.

• Pre-stressing does not change K_{IC} or the flaws; it only lowers the net tension at the surface, so it fails if service damage cuts deeper than the compressive layer.
  • Tempered glass cannot be cut or drilled afterwards; shape it first.
  • For deflection, the gain depends on particle shape and volume fraction, not particle size (Faber-Evans analysis).

7c.html:
The test. A variable (constant) stressing-rate test, also called a dynamic fatigue test, breaks sets of flexure bars at several constant stress rates \dot{\sigma} spread over several decades (for example 0.01 to 100 MPa/s), in the environment of interest (water, humid air, high temperature).

Why strength depends on rate. Ceramics contain subcritical cracks that grow slowly under load by stress corrosion (static fatigue), at a velocity

v = \frac{dc}{dt} = A K_I^{\,n}, \qquad K_I = Y\sigma\sqrt{c}

At a slow rate the cracks have longer to grow before K_I reaches K_{IC}, so the measured strength is lower. Integrating with \sigma = \dot{\sigma}t:

\sigma_f^{\,n+1} = B(n+1)\,\sigma_i^{\,n-2}\,\dot{\sigma} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \log\sigma_f = \frac{1}{n+1}\log\dot{\sigma} + \text{const}

where \sigma_i is the inert strength (no crack growth) and B = 2/[AY^2(n-2)K_{IC}^{\,n-2}].

Information obtained

  1. Crack-growth exponent n from the slope 1/(n+1): the susceptibility to slow crack growth. Glass in water has n \approx 16 (1000 times slower loading lowers strength by 10^{3/17}, about 33 %); n \approx 50 gives only 13 %.
  2. Constant B (or A) from the intercept and \sigma_i, so the full crack-velocity law.
  3. Lifetime and design stress under static load, t_f = B\sigma_i^{\,n-2}\sigma^{-n}; with Weibull statistics this gives stress-probability-time (SPT) diagrams and proof-test levels.
  4. Effect of environment and temperature (humidity, water, heat) on strength, and ranking of materials, much faster than static-fatigue tests lasting months.
pts: Describes the test: fracture (flexure) strength measured at several constant stressing rates over decades, in a fixed environment
Explains that strength falls at lower rates because subcritical cracks grow by stress corrosion, v = AK_I^{\,n}, before K_{IC} is reached
Gives \sigma_f^{\,n+1} \propto \dot{\sigma}, so a log-log plot is a straight line of slope 1/(n+1)
Information 1: the crack-growth exponent n (susceptibility to slow crack growth), with a typical value or comparison
Information 2: the constant B (or A) from the intercept with the inert strength
Information 3: lifetime prediction under static load, t_f = B\sigma_i^{\,n-2}\sigma^{-n}, SPT diagram, design or proof-test stress
Information 4: effect of environment or temperature, quicker than static-fatigue tests

7c.watch:
• K_{IC} does not change with loading rate; the measured strength falls only because the flaws grow during slow loading.
  • The analysis assumes one flaw population and failure by slow crack growth; at high temperature, creep and crack blunting can make strength rise or bend the line.
  • The method is standardised for advanced ceramics as constant stress-rate flexural testing (ASTM C1368 at room temperature, C1465 at high temperature).

8a.html:
Both are ordered states produced by a negative exchange integral (J < 0), usually by superexchange through \mathrm{O^{2-}} in oxides. The moments split into two sublattices pointing in opposite directions.

Antiferromagnetism. The two sublattices carry equal and opposite moments, so they cancel exactly and M = 0 in zero field. Order sets in below the Neel temperature T_N; above it the material is paramagnetic, and the susceptibility shows a cusp at T_N. Example: MnO (T_N = 122 K), NiO (523 K), CoO (293 K) and FeO (198 K) have the rocksalt structure. The 180^\circ M-O-M superexchange makes the moments in each {111} plane parallel and those in adjacent {111} planes antiparallel. Neutron diffraction shows extra reflections below T_N: the magnetic cell is twice the chemical cell. Hematite, \alpha\text{-}\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}, is another example.

Ferrimagnetism. The two sublattices are antiparallel but carry unequal moments, so they cancel only partly and give a spontaneous net magnetisation, with domains and hysteresis as in a ferromagnet. It is lost above the Curie temperature. Example: magnetite, \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}Fe^{3+}}]\mathrm{O_4}, an inverse spinel. A-site \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} (5\,\mu_B) is antiparallel to B-site \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} (4 + 5\,\mu_B), leaving 4\,\mu_B per formula unit. Others: \mathrm{NiFe_2O_4} (2\,\mu_B), YIG \mathrm{Y_3Fe_5O_{12}} (3 tetrahedral against 2 octahedral \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}, 5\,\mu_B) and hard \mathrm{BaFe_{12}O_{19}}. Being oxides, ferrites have high resistivity, so they are used in high-frequency cores and microwave devices.

8b.html:
What m measures. In P_f = 1 - \exp[-(\sigma/\sigma_0)^m], m is the slope of the Weibull plot: a high m means a narrow strength band and a reliable ceramic (slide 11). Each specimen fails from its worst flaw, \sigma_f = K_{IC}/(Y\sqrt{\pi c}), so m is set by how widely the critical flaw size c varies from piece to piece. Ceramics have m \approx 5 to 20; steels about 100.

Factors

  1. Processing and microstructure. Agglomerated or wide-size powders, uneven green density, abnormal grain growth, large pores and inclusions widen the flaw distribution. Fine, uniform, fully dense microstructures (colloidal forming, hot pressing) raise m.
  2. Surface finish. Grinding, scratches and handling add surface cracks; polishing, chamfered edges or annealing out machining damage raise m.
  3. More than one flaw population. Pores, inclusions and machining cracks follow different distributions, so the plot bends into two slopes and one m no longer describes the material (Carter Fig 16.24).
  4. Toughening (R-curve). Transformation toughening, crack bridging or elongated grains make toughness rise as the crack grows, so strength becomes insensitive to flaw size and m rises. In a truly brittle (flat R-curve) ceramic, a higher K_{IC} scales every strength by the same factor and leaves m unchanged.
  5. Service and environment. Slow crack growth in moisture, oxidation, corrosion and thermal shock create or grow flaws and spread the distribution; proof testing removes the weak tail.
  6. Testing and statistics. At least 30 specimens are needed for m within about 20 %; test conditions (stress rate, humidity, alignment) must match service. Specimen volume shifts \sigma_0, not m.

Surface condition: machining or handling flaws lower m; polishing or removing damage raises it
Several flaw populations (volume and surface) give a bent Weibull plot with two slopes
Rising R-curve toughening makes strength flaw-tolerant and raises m; a higher K_{IC} alone in a flat-R-curve ceramic leaves m unchanged

Statistical and test factors: enough specimens (about 30 or more), matched test conditions; volume changes \sigma_0 but not m

8c.html:
Given: P_f = 0.20 at \sigma_1 = 207\ \mathrm{MPa}; P_f = 0.08 at \sigma_2 = 198\ \mathrm{MPa}; allowed P_f = 1/1000 = 0.001.

Find: the Weibull modulus m and the stress \sigma_3 for P_f = 0.001.

Solution. Two-parameter Weibull (slide 11), same specimen volume and loading in test and service:

P_f = 1 - \exp\left[-\left(\frac{\sigma}{\sigma_0}\right)^m\right] \quad\Rightarrow\quad \ln\ln\frac{1}{1 - P_f} = m\ln\sigma - m\ln\sigma_0

Step 1, the two points.

\begin{aligned} \ln\ln\frac{1}{0.80} &= \ln(0.22314) = -1.4999 \\ \ln\ln\frac{1}{0.92} &= \ln(0.08338) = -2.4843 \end{aligned}

Step 2, the modulus (slope).

m = \frac{-1.4999 - (-2.4843)}{\ln 207 - \ln 198} = \frac{0.9844}{0.04445} = 22.1

Step 3, characteristic strength.

\ln\sigma_0 = \ln 207 + \frac{1.4999}{22.1} = 5.3327 + 0.0677 = 5.4005 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \sigma_0 = 221.5\ \mathrm{MPa}

Step 4, allowable stress. For P_f = 0.001, \ln\ln(1/0.999) = \ln(1.0005\times10^{-3}) = -6.9073:

\begin{aligned} \ln\sigma_3 &= 5.4005 - \frac{6.9073}{22.1} = 5.4005 - 0.3119 = 5.0885 \\ \sigma_3 &= 162\ \mathrm{MPa} \end{aligned}

Check by ratio: (\sigma_3/207)^{22.1} = 1.0005\times10^{-3}/0.22314 = 4.48\times10^{-3}, so \sigma_3 = 207 \times 0.783 = 162\ \mathrm{MPa}.

Answer: m \approx 22 and the maximum allowable stress is about 162 MPa (78 % of 207 MPa), with \sigma_0 = 221.5\ \mathrm{MPa}.

8c.watch:
• Use P_s = 0.80 and 0.92, not 0.20 and 0.08, inside \ln\ln(1/P_s); mixing them gives a negative slope.
